memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: The king, moreover, must not acquire great numbers of horses for himself or make the people return to Egypt to get more of them, for the Lord has said to you, "You are not to go back that way again." He must not take many wives, or his heart will be led astray. He must not accumulate large amounts of silver and gold. - Deut 17:16-17 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
God set clear limits on Israel's future king. He was not to amass horses, which meant military might; not to take many wives, which would divide his heart; and not to pile up silver and gold, which breeds greed and pride. Each restriction guarded the king from the three great temptations of power, self-reliant strength, divided affection, and love of wealth.

Behind each limit was a deeper concern, the king's heart. God knew that horses could tempt a king to trust his army instead of the Lord, that many wives would pull his heart toward other gods, and that riches would puff him up. The warning "his heart will be led astray" is the key. God cared less about the king's stable and treasury than about his soul.

Sadly, Solomon later broke every one of these commands, and his heart was indeed led astray. But these temptations are not only for kings. We are all tempted to trust our own strength, to let our affections wander, and to chase wealth. Jesus warned that we cannot serve both God and money (Matt 6:24). The safest place for our hearts is full trust in God alone. Christ, our true King, had no earthly army, no wealth, no divided heart, only perfect devotion to His Father. Which of these three temptations most pulls at your heart today?

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you trust your own strength more than God?
2. What divides your affection away from the Lord?
3. How does the love of money tug at your heart?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, guard my heart from trusting in my own strength or chasing wealth. Keep my affections wholly fixed on You. Amen.
